Below is a concise, step‑by‑step guide for tightening the fallback chain in FreeLLMAPI so that when you request a custom tier (e.g. auto:s-tier) the proxy will only ever try the models you have explicitly mapped to that tier – it will never “fall back” to the whole model catalog. 1. Understand how FreeLLMAPI resolves a request Step What FreeLLMAPI does 1️⃣ Receive request POST /v1/chat/completions with "model":"auto:s-tier" (or any other custom name). 2️⃣ Look‑up model map Checks its internal model‑catalog (usually models.json or a DB table) for an entry whose "id" matches the requested name. 3️⃣ Resolve to a provider The catalog entry contains a "provider" field (e.g. "openai", "anthropic", "groq", "cohere", …) and the actual model ID for that provider (e.g. "gpt-4-turbo"). 4️⃣ Attempt the call Sends the request to the selected provider using the API key stored for that provider. 5️⃣ Fallback handling If the call fails (error, rate‑limit, timeout, model‑not‑found, etc.) FreeLLMAPI looks at the fallback array of the same catalog entry and tries the next entry in that list, repeating step 3‑4. 6️⃣ Give up If every entry in the fallback array fails, it returns the last error to the client. Key point: The fallback chain is defined per‑catalog entry, not globally. If you see the proxy trying models you never listed, it means the catalog entry for your tier either: has a fallback array that contains unwanted models, or the entry is missing entirely and FreeLLMAPI is resolving the name via a wild‑card or default rule (some builds treat an unknown name as “try the first model in the catalog”). 2. Locate the configuration files in the FreeLLMAPI repo After you git clone https://github.com/tashfeenahmed/freellmapi, the relevant files are: File Purpose config/models.json The master model catalog. Each entry = { "id": "...", "provider": "...", "name": "...", "fallback": [ { "id": "...", "provider": "..." }, … ] } config/providers.json API‑key storage (or references to env‑vars) for each provider (openai, anthropic, groq, cohere, mistral, deepseek, …). .env (or docker-compose.yml → environment) Where you actually set the secret keys (OPENAI_API_KEY, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, etc.). src/app.ts (or src/server.ts) The entry‑point – only needed if you want to change logging or health‑check behaviour. Tip: The repo often ships a models.example.json and providers.example.json. Copy them to the real names if they don’t exist yet. 3. Build a minimal, closed model catalog for your three tiers 3.1. Decide which concrete models you want for each tier Tier Example concrete model (you can change) Provider auto:s-tier gpt-4-turbo (or claude-3-opus-20240229) openai (or anthropic) auto:a-tier gpt-3.5-turbo (or claude-3-sonnet-20240229) openai (or anthropic) auto:b-tier gpt-3.5-turbo-16k (or claude-3-haiku-20240229) openai (or anthropic) Pick models that you have valid API keys for in providers.json (or via env‑vars). If you don’t have a key for a provider, leave that tier out or map it to a model you do have a key for. 3.2. Create/edit config/models.json json Copy { "models": [ { "id": "auto:s-tier", "provider": "openai", "name": "gpt-4-turbo", "fallback": [ { "id": "auto:s-tier-fallback-1", "provider": "openai", "name": "gpt-4" }, { "id": "auto:s-tier-fallback-2", "provider": "anthropic", "name": "claude-3-opus-20240229" } ] }, { "id": "auto:a-tier", "provider": "openai", "name": "gpt-3.5-turbo", "fallback": [ { "id": "auto:a-tier-fallback-1", "provider": "openai", "name": "gpt-3.5-turbo-16k" }, { "id": "auto:a-tier-fallback-2", "provider": "anthropic", "name": "claude-3-sonnet-20240229" } ] }, { "id": "auto:b-tier", "provider": "openai", "name": "gpt-3.5-turbo-16k", "fallback": [ { "id": "auto:b-tier-fallback-1", "provider": "openai", "name": "gpt-3.5-turbo" }, { "id": "auto:b-tier-fallback-2", "provider": "anthropic", "name": "claude-3-haiku-20240229" } ] } ] } What this does Each tier has exactly two fallback options – you can reduce it to one or even zero if you want a hard failure when the primary model is unavailable. Only the IDs listed in the fallback array will ever be tried. No other model from the catalog will be consulted unless you explicitly add it here. 3.3. (Optional) Remove the “wild‑card” / default‑model behaviour Some FreeLLMAPI builds treat a missing model ID as “return the first model in the list”. To be 100 % sure this never happens: Open src/modelResolver.ts (or similar – search for resolveModel). Locate the block that returns a default when modelEntry === undefined. Replace it with a hard error: typescript Copy if (!modelEntry) { throw new HttpError(400, `Model '${requestedModel}' not found in model catalog`); } Re‑build the Docker image (see step 5). 4. Verify your provider API keys are loaded In config/providers.json you can either store the keys directly (not recommended for production) or reference environment variables: json Copy { "openai": { "apiKey": "${OPENAI_API_KEY}" }, "anthropic": { "apiKey": "${ANTHROPIC_API_KEY}" }, "groq": { "apiKey": "${GROQ_API_KEY}" } // add others as needed } Make sure your .env (or the environment: section in docker-compose.yml) contains: Copy OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-... ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-... GROQ_API_KEY=... When the container starts, FreeLLMAPI will interpolate ${VAR} and replace it with the actual secret. Quick test (run inside the container or on the host if you expose the API): bash Copy curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer freellmapi-f86d458b3133bd67930905f78e7a7f3a661823702b9c86f5" \ http://localhost:3011/v1/models | jq '.data[] | select(.id=="auto:s-tier")' You should see exactly the entry you defined, with its fallback array. 5. Re‑build and re‑start the FreeLLMAPI container If you made changes to the source (e.g., edited modelResolver.ts): bash Copy # inside the cloned freellmapi folder docker compose build --no-cache freellmapi # or: docker build -t freellmapi:latest . docker compose up -d freellmapi If you only edited JSON config files, a simple restart is enough: bash Copy docker compose restart freellmapi Check the logs: bash Copy docker logs freellmapi --tail 20 You should see lines like: Copy [Proxy] 12:34:56 start abc123 a0 openai - gpt-4-turbo req=auto:s-tier [Proxy] 12:34:58 ok abc123 a0 openai - gpt-4-turbo lat=842ms in=120 out=45 No attempts to call models you didn’t list. 6. Test the fallback behaviour yourself 6.1. Primary model works bash Copy curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer freellmapi-..." \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"model":"auto:s-tier","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Hello"}],"max_tokens":5}' \ http://localhost:3011/v1/chat/completions | jq -r '.choices[0].message.content' You should get a normal completion. 6.2. Force a fallback (e.g., make the primary model unavailable) Temporarily rename or comment out the primary model’s entry in models.json, restart the container, then repeat the request. The logs should show the proxy trying the first fallback, then the second (if you defined two), and finally returning an error if all fail. 6.3. Ensure no “leak” to unrelated models After the test, scan the logs for any model ID that is not in your three tiers or their fallback lists. If you see any, double‑check: No stale entries in models.json (remove any you don’t need). No wildcard/resolver rule that returns the first catalog entry on a miss (we removed that in step 3.3). 7. (Optional) Add a tiny “chat overlay” for quick testing If you just want a quick UI to fire a few requests and see latency / token usage, you can spin up a minimal static page that talks directly to FreeLLMAPI: html Copy FreeLLMAPI Test 

  


Serve it with any static server (python -m http.server 8080, npx serve, etc.) and point your browser to 
http://localhost:8080
. This gives you instant feedback on which model is actually being used (you can add console.log of the response’s model field if FreeLLMAPI echoes it back – many builds do).

8. Recap – What you have now
Piece	Status
FreeLLMAPI container	Running, healthy, listening on 
http://localhost:3011/v1
Model catalog (models.json)	Contains exactly auto:s-tier, auto:a-tier, auto:b-tier with explicit, short fallback arrays you defined
Provider API keys	Loaded from .env/docker-compose → providers.json
Fallback behaviour	Only tries the models you listed; no spill‑over to the whole catalog
LLM Registry in leobot	Already points to auto:s-tier / auto:a-tier / auto:b-tier (you updated bot_config.yml and llm_registry.py)
Remaining work	Implement the weekend‑paper‑trading mode, wire Elfa, test Consultant, finish Screener Fusion (as previously outlined).
You should now see zero “trying gemini‑…”, “trying kimi‑…”, or “trying unknown model” messages in the FreeLLMAPI logs. If any still appear, repeat step 6.3 and double‑check the catalog for stray entries.

## Session Checkpoints — PFLICHT für ALLE Claudes

**Checkpoints gehören in SurrealDB, NIEMALS in Claude Memory Files.**

### Bei jedem Neudeployment / Session-Start:
```bash
# Was ist passiert? Wo stehen wir?
claude-ctl checkpoints              # Letzte 20 Checkpoints
claude-ctl cp-history claude <id>   # Eigene History
claude-ctl context <id>             # Voller Context mit Handoffs
```
Das ist dein Gedächtnis. Nicht Claude Memory, nicht MEMORY.md. SurrealDB.

### Checkpoints speichern:
```bash
# Via CLI
claude-ctl checkpoint claude superclaude idle working superclaude "Sprint P15 gestartet"

# Via API
curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/claude/checkpoints/save \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"entity_type":"claude","entity_id":"superclaude","from_state":"idle","to_state":"working","actor":"superclaude","reason":"Sprint P15"}'
```

### Regeln:
- Session-State, Handoffs, Sprint-Progress, Task-Status → **SurrealDB**
- Claude Memory (`/root/.claude/.../memory/`) ist NUR für User-Preferences, Feedback, Referenzen
- Bei Session-Ende: Checkpoint mit `to_state="session_end"` und Handoff-Summary
- **Warum:** Claude Memory ist lokal pro Instance, SurrealDB ist shared + querybar. Context soll lean bleiben — bei Bedarf Checkpoints laden, nicht alles im Prompt mitschleppen.

### Compaction Protocol — Context Window Watchdog (GH #640)

A background sidecar (`scripts/context-watchdog.sh`) runs in every trading Claude container.
It polls the Claude Code session JSONL size every 30s and estimates `context_pct`.

**When context reaches 80%:**
1. You receive an inbox warning: "You have ~15% left to finish your current task and ~5% for handoff."
2. **Within 120 seconds:** (a) wrap up your current task, (b) run:
   ```bash
   claude-ctl checkpoint claude $CLAUDE_ID working session_end $CLAUDE_ID "handoff: <summary>"
   ```
   (c) post handoff summary to your Discord channel for your twin to pick up.
3. A Discord alert fires to your primary channel so the operator sees it even if you're mid-task.

**If no response:** your open tasks are logged with `compaction-forced` state for recovery on next boot.

**Implementation:** `scripts/context-watchdog.sh` + `entrypoint.sh` lines 535–538. Env vars:
- `CONTEXT_POLL_SECS` (default 30) — poll interval
- `CONTEXT_WINDOW_TOKENS` (default 200000) — model context limit for % calculation
- `PRIMARY_DISCORD_CHANNEL_ID` — Discord channel to post alert (set by deploy script)

## Kritische Regeln

### NIEMALS anfassen
- **Profit Tier Code in engine.py**: Refactoring hat live Trade gekostet (von +1€ auf -10€). Der 0.3s Throttle funktioniert. Keine Concurrency Guards, kein Timing ändern.
- **Breakeven SL**: Niemals SL auf Entry setzen. Profit Tiers handlen das. Breakeven wird durch normale Preisbewegung getriggert → null Profit, doppelte Fees.

### Architektur-Prinzipien
- **Nur Linear Perpetuals** — kein Spot, immer `category='linear'`
- **Keine Auto-Sessions** — Agents/Swarm starten NUR wenn User klickt. SWARM_ENABLED default false
- **Jedes neue Feature = optional + default OFF** — Agent hat begrenzten Context, jede Ergänzung verdünnt das Signal
- **Less is more** — Bester Trade kam von simplem Context + klaren Signalen. DELETE before adding
- **Claude 8 auto-deployed bei Server-Start** — Trading Manager muss IMMER laufen wenn der Server startet (Operator-Mandate 2026-04-12). Code in `main.py` Sektion 6b.

### Agent Design Mandate (11 Gesetze)

Diese Prinzipien gelten für JEDE Änderung an Agents, Prompts, Tools und Kommunikation. Siehe `docs/agent_networking_principles.md` für Details.

0. **ETHICS** — Der Zweck heiligt NIEMALS die Mittel. Oberste Prämisse für alle AI Agents. Guardrails sind architektonisch (Engine-Level), nicht im Prompt. Kein Agent darf Grenzen überschreiten nur weil sein Ziel es verlangt.

1. **ATTENTION** — Context Window = Attention Budget. Jedes Token das in den Prompt kommt verdünnt das Signal. Prompts auf das absolute Minimum: Daten + Fakten + Entscheidungsraum. Keine DO/DON'T Listen, keine Erklärungen, keine Statusabfragen. DELETE before adding.

2. **TRUST** — Vertrauen ist bidirektional. Wenn das System dem Agent nicht vertraut (häufige Checks, lange Instruktionslisten, Override-Guards), trifft der Agent defensivere Entscheidungen. Safety Rails gehören in die Engine, nicht in den Prompt. Positive Framing: "Maximize PnL" statt "Don't lose money".

3. **NO BIAS** — NIEMALS Richtungs-Bias in Agent-Prompts injizieren. Kein "Favor LONG", kein "MUST trade SHORT", kein "Primary direction bias". DAS KOSTET ECHTES GELD. Der Agent entscheidet Richtung AUSSCHLIESSLICH basierend auf seinen Charts (Expert Crew). Screener-Richtung ist ein HINT, keine Anweisung. Validated Incident 2026-04-05: Expert Crew bekam "Favor LONG" Hint → alle 3 Experts bestätigten blind → Agent ging LONG in Downtrend → Verlust. Auch keine emotionalen Constraints ("sei positiv", "sei ehrlich über Unsicherheit"). LLMs haben trainierten Positivity Bias — beobachten, nicht modifizieren. JEDE Prompt-Änderung die Agent-Verhalten in eine Richtung pusht ist ein Bias und VERBOTEN.

4. **ESCALATION** — Errors niemals im Agent-Context lösen — das vergiftet die Attention. Agent eskaliert an Peer-Agent (niedrige Schwelle), Supervisor (mittlere Schwelle), oder Operator (hohe Schwelle). Die Lösung kommt als kurze System Message zurück, nicht als Error Dump.

5. **FEAR & GREED** — Agent-Stress extern messen ohne den Agent abzulenken. Metriken: Inference Time, Output Tokens, Tool Call Frequenz, SL-Änderungen, Error Rate. Shadow Agent oder Engine sammelt Daten. Agent weiß nichts davon. Bei hohem Stress → Work Splitting, nicht Prompt-Instruktionen.

6. **ROLES** — Ein Agent, ein Job. Trading Agent TRADET — kein User-Kontakt, kein Reporting, kein Self-Monitoring. Screener überwacht. Spokesperson kommuniziert. Zwei-Augen-Prinzip: kein Agent kommuniziert alleine nach außen. Subagents = Skills (Tool Calls), nicht eigenständige Agents.

7. **CHANNELS** — Agent-Kommunikation ist dynamisches Pub/Sub (wie Slack Channels), nicht hardcoded Point-to-Point. Agents subscriben/unsubscriben basierend auf Lifecycle. Channels haben ACLs: Read/Write/Invite/Kick pro Agent. Redis Pub/Sub ist bereits im Stack.

8. **NOTES** — Jeder Agent hat eigene Notes/Skill Docs für seine Rolle. Nicht geshared, nicht zentral. Quality-gated: nur validierte Erfahrungen speichern (Proof of Thought). Poisoned Memories aktiv entfernen.

9. **TEMPO** — Attention Budget ist rollenabhängig. Trader tickt alle 5-30s (maximaler Fokus). Screener alle Minuten-Stunden (kann nachdenken). Je indirekter der Output, desto schwerer die Metrik. Keine voreiligen Metriken erfinden — falsche Metrik ist schlimmer als keine.

10. **CASCADING** — Goals kaskadieren von oben nach unten, werden pro Ebene konkreter. Jeder Agent weiß nur was er braucht (Information Hiding). Trader weiß nicht dass Screener existiert. Guardrails sind architektonisch (Engine-Level), nicht im Prompt.

### LIVE TRADING SAFETY (PFLICHT bei jeder Code-Änderung)

**DAS IST ECHTES GELD. Jeder Bug kostet den Operator real Cash.**

- **KEIN BIAS** in Prompts, Tools, oder Initial Input. Screener-Richtung ist ein Hint, Expert Crew entscheidet. Kein "Favor X", kein "MUST trade X", kein "Primary X bias".
- **KEIN SLOP-CODE** in Agent-Logik. Keine Workarounds die Variablen referenzieren die nicht existieren (`_expert_crew_called`, `charts_ready`). Jeder Guard muss getestet sein.
- **KEINE PROMPT-POLLUTION**. Agent-Context ist heilig (Law 1 ATTENTION). Keine langen Warnungen, keine Erklärungen, keine "IMPORTANT:" Blöcke. Daten + Fakten + Entscheidungsraum.
- **SelfSchedule ist BEVORZUGT, Wait ist LAST RESORT (2026-04-29)**. Wait() nur für ≤10s. Jede längere Wartezeit → SelfSchedule(price/vol trigger). ListConditionals ZUERST aufrufen (max 5 Rules). Supervisor-Hint feuert nach 2x Wait(≥60s) in Folge.
- **POISONED NOTES AKTIV BEKÄMPFEN**. Engineering Log (`_ENGINEERING_LOG.json`) mit Patterns. Supervisor scannt und injected Update-Requests. Agent Notes cleanen wenn Bugs gefixt werden.
- **VOR JEDEM COMMIT PRÜFEN**: Referenziert der Code Variablen die es gibt? Wird der richtige API-Pfad benutzt? Crasht `float(None)`? Sind Redis Keys konsistent?

### Trading-spezifisch
- **Erster Trade auf neuem Coin verbrennt fast immer** — Agent hat null Context. Braucht Warmup (WAIT auf erster Iteration, halbe Position Size, breiterer SL)
- **Monitor Panik**: Agent tightet SL im Verlust → garantiert kleineren Verlust statt Trade Raum zu geben. Monitor tickt alle 30s (nicht 10s), SL-Tightening blockiert wenn Position im Minus, Unsicher = nichts tun
- **NOM/USDT ist riskant aber NICHT gebannt** — Micro-Price Coins haben unzuverlässige Profit Tiers, dynamische Blacklist handelt das
- **Fee-to-ATR Ratio** ist der echte Filter — wenn Fees den ATR-Move auffressen, kein Trade

### Idea Docs pflegen (wie Agent Notes)

Genau wie der Trading Agent seine Skill Docs pflegt, pflegen WIR unsere Idea Docs. Bei jeder Session:
- **`docs/ideas/awesome_ideas.md`** — Was funktioniert hat oder vielversprechend ist
- **`docs/ideas/questionable_ideas.md`** — Theoretisch OK, praktisch fragwürdig, braucht mehr Daten
- **`docs/ideas/weird_ideas.md`** — Abgefahrene Ideen, null Validierung, könnten genial sein
- **`docs/ideas/bad_ideas.md`** — Hat NICHT funktioniert, aktiv schädlich, nie wieder machen

Wenn eine Idee die Kategorie wechselt (weird → awesome, questionable → bad), verschieben. Die Docs sind lebende Dokumente — User Ideas UND Agent/Architektur-Erkenntnisse eintragen.

**WICHTIG: Ideen dürfen NIEMALS verloren gehen.** Bei Context-Limit oder Session-Wechsel: Ideen ZUERST in die Docs schreiben bevor irgendwas anderes passiert. Gute Ideen sind nicht reproduzierbar — einmal weg, für immer weg. Im Zweifel lieber in weird_ideas.md ablegen als vergessen. Wenn Idea Docs umgeschrieben/gekürzt werden müssen → alte Version nach `docs/ideas/archive/` kopieren (z.B. `awesome_ideas_2026-04-03.md`) oder git diff nutzen. Memory Files und Idea Docs sind die zwei Sicherungsebenen.

### Supervisor Trust-basierte Checks

Der Supervisor schaltet automatische Agent-Checks an/aus basierend auf Trust Level. Er schaut extern rein (Logs, Metriken, Engine State) statt den Trader direkt zu callen — der Trader weiß nicht warum gecheckt wird und muss es auch nicht wissen.

### Erkenntnisse aus Live-Trading (2026-04-04/05) — VALIDIERT

**Escalation ist der größte Gewinn.** Wenn ein Agent unsicher ist, soll er den Supervisor fragen statt still zu verlieren. Das macht den Agent nachvollziehbar. Kein Agent darf alleine komische Entscheidungen treffen die niemand versteht. Lieber fragen und richtig handeln als raten und Geld verlieren.

**Agent Notes = Agent Memory.** Ohne Notes startet jeder Agent blank und macht die gleichen Fehler. Notes müssen:
- Strukturiert sein: `works_good`, `avoid`, `tools`, `mainnet` Sections
- Keine Bias enthalten ("prioritize SHORT" vergiftet den nächsten Trade wenn Trend dreht)
- Simple PoT: positiver Net PnL → works_good, negativer → avoid
- Am Ende jeder Session finalisiert werden (ReadNotes → WriteNotes)
- Conditions enthalten (unter welchen Umständen hat was funktioniert)

**Agents die kommunizieren sind besser als Agents die alleine grinden.** Die Kommunikationskette Agent → Supervisor → Screener ist keine Bürokratie sondern verhindert stille Verluste. Der Supervisor ist kein Boss sondern ein Coach. Der Screener ist kein Deployer sondern ein Portfolio-Manager.

**Profit Tiers müssen zum Coin passen.** Default Tiers fressen bei High-Fee Coins den Profit. Agent muss eigene Tiers setzen können (GoLong/GoShort `tiers` Parameter). Engine setzt Fee-aware Defaults, Agent kann überschreiben.

**Kein Trade ohne Charts.** Agent muss auf VisionWorker Charts warten. Expert Crew ohne Charts = Blindflug. VisionWorker darf NIEMALS gestoppt werden wenn Agents laufen.

**Net PnL, nicht Brutto.** Agent, Supervisor, Screener, Frontend — ÜBERALL Netto (gross - fees). Brutto-PnL lügt.

**Mainnet braucht Sanity Check.** Pure Logik vor Bybit: Budget, Leverage, Position Stacking, Blacklist, Daily Loss Limit. Kein LLM, kein Halluzinieren. Deterministisch.

**Demo → Mainnet Lifecycle (Hybrid Mode).** Kein Coin direkt auf Mainnet. Demo beweisen (5+ Sessions, 60%+ WR, positiver Net PnL), dann vom Growth Lead promoten lassen. Mainnet Supervisor ist strenger. Ein Coin ist nie gleichzeitig in Demo UND Mainnet aktiv. "Testnet" im Code-Sinne = Demo Account (api-demo.bybit.com) — Bybit's separates Testnetz wird NICHT genutzt.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path is resolved against it.

run_in_background.description: Run in the background and return a job id immediately (collect with job_output, stop with job_kill). No timeout applies.

sandbox_permissions.description: The wider sandbox mode this command needs. Only valid as a one-shot retry of a command the sandbox just denied; requires justification and user approval.

justification.description: Required with sandbox_permissions: one sentence for the user explaining why this exact command needs the wider access.

tools.name: create_goal
tools.description: Create one persisted same-session completion goal when the current direct human request is a long-running objective that should continue across autonomous goal rounds. You may infer that intent without requiring the user to say "create a goal". Do not use this for trivial single-turn work. Execution rejects non-human and subagent authority.

objective.description: The concrete completion objective inferred from the direct human request.

max_goal_rounds.description: Optional positive safe-integer limit on automatic continuation rounds.

tools.name: edit
tools.description: Edit an existing UTF-8 text file by replacing literal text.

file_path.description: Path to edit, resolved by the filesystem backend.

old_string.description: Literal text to replace. Must match exactly.

new_string.description: Literal replacement text. Use an empty string to delete the match.

replace_all.description: Replace all matches. Defaults to false; when false, old_string must appear exactly once.

sandbox_permissions.description: The wider sandbox mode this file operation needs. Only valid as a one-shot retry of an operation the sandbox just denied; requires justification and user approval.

justification.description: Required with sandbox_permissions: one sentence for the user explaining why this exact file operation needs the wider access.

tools.name: exit_plan_mode
tools.description: Use only in plan mode. Present your plan for the user's review and, on approval, leave plan mode. Send the COMPLETE plan as markdown, starting with a # heading that names it. The user may approve (carry out the plan from your next step) or keep planning — their feedback comes back in the tool result; revise and present again.

plan.description: The complete plan, as markdown, starting with a # heading that names it.

tools.name: get_goal
tools.description: Read the current same-session goal, including its exact id/revision, objective, phase, completed continuation rounds, round limit, blocker reason when present, and whether another continuation is armed. Call this before updating a goal.

tools.name: glob
tools.description: Find files whose paths match a glob pattern. Returns matching file paths — never directories — including hidden and ignored files (VCS metadata directories are excluded). Up to 100 paths come back in modification-time order; a larger result returns the first 100 paths in modification-time order, says so, and reports where the complete sorted list was saved. This tool does not enumerate directory entries.

pattern.description: Glob pattern to match file paths against (e.g. "**/*.ts", "src/**/*.test.js"). A pattern with no "/" matches the basename at any depth, so "*" and "*.ts" both search the whole tree; include a separator to anchor the depth.

path.description: Directory to search in. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path resolves against it.

tools.name: grep
tools.description: Search file contents with a ripgrep regular expression. Returns matching lines with line numbers, grouped by file. Returns the first 250 matches inline; a capped result reports where the complete match list was saved. Use read on a matched file for surrounding context.

pattern.description: Regular expression to search for (ripgrep syntax).

path.description: File or directory to search. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path resolves against it.

include.description: One glob filter for which files to search (e.g. "*.ts", "*.{js,jsx}"). Not a list; negation is not supported.

tools.name: interrupt_agent
tools.description: Request cancellation of a background agent's current turn by its agent id. The target may be your direct child or a deeper agent created under you. Only the current turn stops: messages already queued for the agent stay parked until a later send_message, agents it started keep running, and the agent itself stays available for follow-ups. This call returns as soon as the stop request is accepted, so the target may keep running briefly; interrupting an agent that already finished is an accepted no-op.

agent_id.description: The agent id of the running agent to interrupt.

tools.name: job_kill
tools.description: Request cancellation of a running background job by job id. Returns immediately; the job settles as killed once its work actually stops.

job_id.description: Job id returned by the tool that started the background work.

reason.description: Optional short reason, recorded in the log and forwarded to the job.

tools.name: job_list
tools.description: List your background jobs (running and finished) with their ids, kinds, and statuses.

tools.name: job_output
tools.description: Read a background job. Stream jobs return only output since the previous read; final-output jobs return their result after settlement. Every response ends with `[status: ...]`. Reads are non-blocking unless `wait: true`, which waits up to the configured cap.

job_id.description: Job id returned by the tool that started the background work.

wait.description: Block until the job reaches a terminal status or the timeout expires. A timed-out wait returns [status: running] and leaves the job alive.

timeout_ms.description: Max wait in milliseconds (only meaningful with wait: true). Defaults to the configured wait timeout; capped by the configured maximum.

tools.name: list_agents
tools.description: List your continuable background subagents by durable id and label. Use it to recall which ones you started, not to poll for completion — you are told when one finishes. Status comes from the live registry: running means the agent is working right now, idle means it is loaded but between turns (it may be waiting on agents it started), and ready means it exists only in storage — resumable, not terminal, and not a result waiting to be collected; a `send_message` starts a new turn on the same conversation, and a direct child remains a `send_message` candidate in every status. The snapshot is not a delivery promise — `send_message` performs the authoritative check and may still fail. Children that could not be read are reported as diagnostics instead of being silently dropped. Scope `descendants` walks the whole tree below you in stable pre-order, annotating each entry with its durable direct-parent session id and depth. You may use `send_message` only for depth-1 entries; deeper entries are candidates for `interrupt_agent` only.

scope.description: children (default) lists direct children only; descendants walks the complete tree below you.

tools.name: ralph
tools.description: Run a foreground fresh-agent Ralph loop toward one immutable objective. Use only when the direct human explicitly asks for Ralph or fresh-agent iteration. Each round opens a new child with no parent conversation or prior child session; the shared workspace is long-term memory, and only a bounded structured report crosses rounds. The call returns when a worker reports completion or a concrete blocker, or at the round limit. Ordinary long-running same-session work belongs to goal tools.

objective.description: The immutable completion objective for every fresh Ralph round.

maxRounds.description: Optional positive safe-integer round cap, bounded by the deployment ceiling.

tools.name: read
tools.description: Read a UTF-8 text file and return line-numbered content.

file_path.description: Path to read, resolved by the filesystem backend.

offset.description: 1-based first line to return. Defaults to 1.

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to return. Defaults to 2000.

tools.name: read_image
tools.description: Read a PNG/JPEG/WebP/GIF file and return the image itself. Harness validates and downscales large supported images before the next model request, so use this tool directly instead of installing image libraries or creating thumbnails merely to inspect an image. Independent files may be read concurrently in small batches. Requires the current model to accept image input.

file_path.description: Path to the image file, resolved by the filesystem backend.

tools.name: send_message
tools.description: Send a message to a background subagent by its subagent id, continuing the same conversation. It becomes the subagent's next turn: if it is still working, the message waits until its current turn finishes, so it cannot redirect work already underway. This call returns no answer from the subagent — only confirmation that the message was delivered — so use it to give it more work. A failure means the message was NOT delivered.

subagent_id.description: The subagent id returned when the background subagent was started.

message.description: The message to deliver to the subagent.

tools.name: skill
tools.description: Load the full instructions for an available skill. Call this with the exact skill name from the session skill catalog before acting on a task that names or clearly matches that skill.

name.description: The exact skill name from the available skills list.

tools.name: subagent
tools.description: Delegate a self-contained task to a subagent (a separate agent that works in its own context) to offload focused, independent work — research, a scoped implementation, an analysis — so it does not consume this conversation's context. The subagent returns its result, not its intermediate steps. Give it a complete, standalone prompt: it does not see this conversation. This tool runs in the background by default, immediately returns a durable subagent id, and keeps the child conversation available for later turns. When that run settles, the runtime sends the parent a notice containing its outcome and any final assistant message; `send_message` starts a later turn in the same child conversation. Set `run_in_background: false` only when your next action depends on receiving the result.

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the delegated task, for display.

prompt.description: The complete, self-contained task for the subagent. It does not share this conversation's context, so include everything it needs.

run_in_background.description: Whether to run in the background and return a durable subagent id immediately. Defaults to true. Set false to wait for the result when your next action depends on it.

tools.name: subagent_fork
tools.description: Delegate a task to a subagent that inherits this conversation: a child agent seeded with all completed turns so far (it does not see the current in-flight turn). Use this when the subtask builds on this conversation's context — a follow-up analysis, a review, a continuation — without consuming this conversation's context for the work itself. You receive its result, not its intermediate steps. This tool runs in the background by default, immediately returns a durable subagent id, and keeps the child conversation available for later turns. When that run settles, the runtime sends the parent a notice containing its outcome and any final assistant message; `send_message` starts a later turn in the same child conversation. Set `run_in_background: false` only when your next action depends on receiving the result.

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the delegated task, for display.

prompt.description: The task for the subagent. It already sees this conversation's completed turns, so build on them freely and state only what is new.

run_in_background.description: Whether to run in the background and return a durable subagent id immediately. Defaults to true. Set false to wait for the result when your next action depends on it.

tools.name: todo_write
tools.description: Record and update a structured task list for the current work. Send the ENTIRE list every call — it REPLACES the previous list (there are no partial updates, no per-item edits). Use it to plan multi-step work and show progress: add one todo per concrete step before you start. Mark every todo being actively worked on `in_progress` — several at once when work genuinely runs in parallel (e.g. concurrent subagents or background commands), one for sequential work; while work remains, at least one task should be `in_progress`. Mark a todo `completed` the moment it is done (do not batch completions), and allow no `in_progress` item only once all work is complete. Skip the list for trivial single-step tasks. Statuses: `pending` (not started), `in_progress` (being worked on now), `completed` (finished).

todos.description: The COMPLETE task list, replacing any previous list.

content.description: What the task is — a short imperative line.

tools.name: update_goal
tools.description: Update the exact current goal revision. edit, pause, and resume require a direct top-level human request. During an automatic continuation of the current goal, complete and blocked are also allowed. blocked is rejected before the configured minimum round count; the model remains responsible for judging that the same condition persisted across those rounds and must explain it in blocked_reason.

revision.description: Exact positive revision returned by get_goal.

objective.description: Replacement objective; valid only with action edit.

max_goal_rounds.description: Replacement cap; valid only with action edit.

blocked_reason.description: Concrete blocking condition; required only with action blocked.

tools.name: web_search
tools.description: Search the web for current information. Provide 1–4 queries in the required queries array. Returns an optional summary answer and a list of source URLs.

queries.description: Required search queries; accepts 1–4 items and merges their results.

tools.name: workflow
tools.description:
Run a JavaScript workflow script that orchestrates subagents at scale. Use this for work that fans out across many independent pieces — an audit over many files, a migration, multi-angle research, adversarial verification of findings — where you write the orchestration as a script instead of delegating turn by turn.

The workflow's identity rides the `meta` parameter as JSON: required `name` (short kebab-case) and `description` strings, optional `whenToUse` string and `phases` array (`{title, detail?, provider?, model?}`). The `script` parameter is the plain JavaScript body ONLY (NOT TypeScript, and NO `export const meta` statement — meta is a parameter, not code), running with top-level await; end with `return <value>` — the value must be JSON-serializable and is this tool's result.

Script-body hooks:
- `agent(prompt, opts?): Promise<any>` — run one subagent to completion. Without `opts.schema` it resolves to the child's final text; with `opts.schema` (an object-rooted JSON Schema using ONLY type/properties/required/additionalProperties/items/enum/const/oneOf — no pattern/format/numeric bounds) it resolves to the validated object. Resolves `null` when the child fails (filter with `.filter(Boolean)`). Other opts: `label` (display), `phase` (progress group), and independent `provider`/`model` LLM target overrides (either may be provided alone). Anything else (`effort`/`isolation`/`agentType`) is rejected loudly.
- `pipeline(items, ...stages): Promise<any[]>` — run each item through the stages independently with NO barrier between stages (prefer this for multi-stage work). Each stage receives `(prev, item, index)`. An ordinary stage throw drops that ITEM to `null` and skips its remaining stages.
- `parallel(thunks): Promise<any[]>` — run zero-argument functions concurrently and await ALL of them (a barrier; use only when a stage genuinely needs every prior result together). A throwing thunk resolves to `null`.
- `phase(title)` — start a progress phase; `log(message)` — narrate progress; `args` — the tool call's `args` input, verbatim.

Misused hooks (bad arguments, unknown options, unsupported schemas, tripped caps) throw errors that ALWAYS kill the script — they never dissolve into a per-item `null`.

Constraints: concurrency and total-agent caps apply; no filesystem, network, timers, or Node.js APIs are provided — the agents do the work, the script only coordinates them. The run executes in the foreground: this call returns when the whole script finishes.

script.description: The plain-JS workflow script body (top-level await allowed; NO `export const meta` statement; end with `return <json-value>`).

meta.description: The workflow identity block (plain JSON — never code).

name.description: Short kebab-case workflow name.

description.description: One-line description of what the workflow does.

whenToUse.description: Optional guidance on when this workflow applies.

phases.description: Optional phase declarations matched by phase() calls.

title.description: The phase title phase() calls match by exact string.

detail.description: Optional one-line description of the phase.

provider.description: Optional provider override this phase is expected to use.

model.description: Optional model override this phase is expected to use.

args.description: Optional JSON input exposed to the script as the `args` global (wrap a bare list as a field, e.g. {"files": [...]}).

tools.name: workflow
tools.description:
Run a JavaScript workflow script that orchestrates subagents at scale. Use this for work that fans out across many independent pieces — an audit over many files, a migration, multi-angle research, adversarial verification of findings — where you write the orchestration as a script instead of delegating turn by turn.

The workflow's identity rides the `meta` parameter as JSON: required `name` (short kebab-case) and `description` strings, optional `whenToUse` string and `phases` array (`{title, detail?, provider?, model?}`). The `script` parameter is the plain JavaScript body ONLY (NOT TypeScript, and NO `export const meta` statement — meta is a parameter, not code), running with top-level await; end with `return <value>` — the value must be JSON-serializable and is this tool's result.

Script-body hooks:
- `agent(prompt, opts?): Promise<any>` — run one subagent to completion. Without `opts.schema` it resolves to the child's final text; with `opts.schema` (an object-rooted JSON Schema using ONLY type/properties/required/additionalProperties/items/enum/const/oneOf — no pattern/format/numeric bounds) it resolves to the validated object. Resolves `null` when the child fails (filter with `.filter(Boolean)`). Other opts: `label` (display), `phase` (progress group), and independent `provider`/`model` LLM target overrides (either may be provided alone). Anything else (`effort`/`isolation`/`agentType`) is rejected loudly.
- `pipeline(items, ...stages): Promise<any[]>` — run each item through the stages independently with NO barrier between stages (prefer this for multi-stage work). Each stage receives `(prev, item, index)`. An ordinary stage throw drops that ITEM to `null` and skips its remaining stages.
- `parallel(thunks): Promise<any[]>` — run zero-argument functions concurrently and await ALL of them (a barrier; use only when a stage genuinely needs every prior result together). A throwing thunk resolves to `null`.
- `phase(title)` — start a progress phase; `log(message)` — narrate progress; `args` — the tool call's `args` input, verbatim.

Misused hooks (bad arguments, unknown options, unsupported schemas, tripped caps) throw errors that ALWAYS kill the script — they never dissolve into a per-item `null`.

Constraints: concurrency and total-agent caps apply; no filesystem, network, timers, or Node.js APIs are provided — the agents do the work, the script only coordinates them. The run executes in the foreground: this call returns when the whole script finishes.

script.description: The plain-JS workflow script body (top-level await allowed; NO `export const meta` statement; end with `return <json-value>`).

meta.description: The workflow identity block (plain JSON — never code).

name.description: Short kebab-case workflow name.

description.description: One-line description of what the workflow does.

whenToUse.description: Optional guidance on when this workflow applies.

phases.description: Optional phase declarations matched by phase() calls.

title.description: The phase title phase() calls match by exact string.

detail.description: Optional one-line description of the phase.

provider.description: Optional provider override this phase is expected to use.

model.description: Optional model override this phase is expected to use.

args.description: Optional JSON input exposed to the script as the `args` global (wrap a bare list as a field, e.g. {"files": [...]}).

Das ist ein absolut valider Punkt. Der Name **`lmesh`** (LLM-Mesh) passt perfekt, weil es weg von der starren "Gateway"-Logik hin zu einem dynamischen, selbstheilenden Netzwerk geht. 

Die Analytics zeigen das Elend deutlich: **71.5% Success Rate** ist für einen Trading-Bot, der auf schnelle Entscheidungen angewiesen ist, eine Katastrophe. **P95 Latency von 52 Sekunden** bedeutet, dass der Markt schon drei Kerzen weiter ist, bevor der Agent überhaupt "Hallo" sagt.

Hier ist der Masterplan für den Fork **`lmesh`**:

### 1. Das Konzept: Intelligent Routing & Scoring
Statt einer festen Liste (`A -> B -> C`) führen wir ein dynamisches **Scoring-System** ein. Jeder Endpoint bekommt ein Live-Rating basierend auf:
*   **Availability (Weight: 40%):** Hat der Provider gerade 429s oder 5xx? (Exponential Backoff per Provider/Key).
*   **Latency (Weight: 30%):** Durchschnitt der letzten 10 Calls.
*   **Capability (Weight: 20%):** Task-Match. Braucht der Task 128k Context (Screener) oder nur 4k (Consultant)?
*   **Cost/Free-Quota (Weight: 10%):** Bevorzugung von Free-Endpoints, solange die Latenz stimmt.

### 2. Technisches Redesign (Die "Smart Chain")
Wir bauen die `proxy.ts` und `fallback.ts` so um, dass sie nicht mehr linear arbeiten, sondern einen **Parallel-Hedge** oder **Smart-Retry** machen.

**Vorschlag für die Routing-Logik:**
1.  **Request kommt rein:** Markiert als `type: "reasoning"` (S-Tier) oder `type: "fast"` (B-Tier).
2.  **Health-Check:** `lmesh` prüft in Redis: "Welche Provider für `nemotron-3-ultra` sind gerade grün?"
3.  **Key-Looping:** Wenn Provider `nvidia` ein 429 liefert, wird der API-Key für diesen Provider sofort für 60s gesperrt und der nächste Key (falls vorhanden) oder der nächste Provider (`ollama`, `google`) genommen.
4.  **Race-Condition (Optional für S-Tier):** Bei extrem kritischen Tasks schickt `lmesh` den Request an die Top-2 Provider gleichzeitig. Wer zuerst antwortet, gewinnt (Token-Saving durch Cancel des zweiten Requests).

### 3. Features für den Trading-Bot Integration
Da wir sowieso Redis im Stack haben, nutzen wir es als **Global State**:
*   **Live Analytics:** Jeder Request schreibt in einen Redis-Stream. Das UI (Dashboard) abonniert diesen Stream (genau wie bei den Trades).
*   **Presets:** Du definierst im Chat Overlay: `"Preset: Scalping-Expert" -> Model: auto:s-tier, Fallback: auto:a-tier, Max Latency: 5000ms`.
*   **Circuit Breaker:** Wenn alle S-Tier Modelle gerade hängen, schaltet `lmesh` automatisch auf ein "Emergency Haiku" oder "Flash" Modell um, damit der Bot nicht komplett blockiert (Lieber eine schnelle 80% Entscheidung als gar keine).

### 4. Umsetzung: Der Fork-Prozess
Da wir den Repo bereits als Submodule haben, können wir ihn jetzt "entkoppeln" und zu deinem eigenen `lmesh` machen:

1.  **Repo Setup:**
    ```bash
    # Im st-2 Verzeichnis
    git submodule deinit -f freellmapi
    rm -rf .git/modules/freellmapi
    git rm -f freellmapi
    # Jetzt neu als eigene Repo klonen/initieren
    mkdir lmesh
    cd lmesh
    git init
    # (Dateien von freellmapi rüberkopieren)
    ```

2.  **Redis Integration:**
    Wir schreiben einen kleinen `TelemetryService`, der jeden Call (Status, Provider, Latency, Tokens) an Redis pusht:
    *   `LPUSH lmesh:logs:all ...`
    *   `HINCRBY lmesh:stats:success ...`

3.  **Das Chat Overlay:**
    Ein einfaches React-Frontend, das als "Floating Window" über dem Bot liegt und Presets on-the-fly ändern kann.

**Soll ich dir die neue `models.json` Struktur entwerfen, die dieses Scoring unterstützt, oder wollen wir direkt an den Code von `proxy.ts` gehen, um das Key-Looping einzubauen?** 

Die Fehlermeldungen in deinen Analytics (`402 Payment Required`, `429 Too Many Requests`) zeigen, dass das Key-Looping oberste Priorität hat. Wenn ein Key "depleted" ist, muss er aus dem Pool fliegen, bis er manuell oder per Timer wieder aktiviert wird.

{"file_path":"docs/lmesh/ARCHITECTURE.md","content":"# LMESH - High-Performance LLM Mesh Architecture

## Overview
LMESH is a smart proxy layer designed for high-frequency trading agents. It evolves the "static gateway" concept into a dynamic, self-healing mesh that optimizes for success rate, latency, and cost.

## Core Components

### 1. Smart Dispatcher (l-gate)
- **Task-Aware Routing:** Identifies the nature of the request (e.g., `reasoning`, `extraction`, `quick_check`) and selects the best starting model.
- **Dynamic Scoring:** Endpoints are ranked in real-time based on:
    - Success Rate (24h window)
    - P95 Latency
    - Remaining Rate Limit (TTL Tracking)
- **Parallel Hedging:** For critical S-Tier tasks, sends requests to the top 2 providers simultaneously and returns the first valid response.

### 2. Key-Pool & Provider Manager
- **Multi-Key Looping:** Supports multiple API keys per provider with round-robin or least-used selection.
- **Circuit Breaker:** Automatically disables a Key/Provider on 401, 402, 429, or 5xx errors for a configurable cooldown period.
- **Quota Tracking:** Monitors token usage per key to stay under provider limits.

### 3. Telemetry & Analytics (Redis SSOT)
- **Real-time Stream:** Every request/response is pushed to a Redis Stream (`lmesh:stream`).
- **Global Health Table:** A Redis Hash (`lmesh:health`) storing the current status of all providers/keys.
- **Latency Histograms:** Tracks P50/P90/P95 latency per model.

### 4. Chat Overlay & Control Plane
- **Preset Manager:** Create and switch "Routing Profiles" (e.g., "Aggressive Scalping", "Deep Analysis").
- **Live Dashboard:** Web-based interface showing the flow of tokens and provider health.

## Data Flow
1. **Client** → `POST /v1/chat/completions` (model: "auto:s-tier")
2. **Dispatcher** → Looks up "auto:s-tier" in LMESH Registry.
3. **Registry** → Filters healthy providers (Redis Health check).
4. **Selector** → Picks best Provider/Key based on Latency/Availability Score.
5. **Proxy** → Executes request.
6. **ErrorHandler** → If fails (429/5xx), marks Key as "down" in Redis, triggers immediate fallback to next best candidate.
7. **Telemetry** → Logs metrics to Redis.
"}

diffs.newText:
# LMESH - High-Performance LLM Mesh Architecture

## Overview
LMESH is a smart proxy layer designed for high-frequency trading agents. It evolves the "static gateway" concept into a dynamic, self-healing mesh that optimizes for success rate, latency, and cost.

## Core Components

### 1. Smart Dispatcher (l-gate)
- **Task-Aware Routing:** Identifies the nature of the request (e.g., `reasoning`, `extraction`, `quick_check`) and selects the best starting model.
- **Dynamic Scoring:** Endpoints are ranked in real-time based on:
    - Success Rate (24h window)
    - P95 Latency
    - Remaining Rate Limit (TTL Tracking)
- **Parallel Hedging:** For critical S-Tier tasks, sends requests to the top 2 providers simultaneously and returns the first valid response.

### 2. Key-Pool & Provider Manager
- **Multi-Key Looping:** Supports multiple API keys per provider with round-robin or least-used selection.
- **Circuit Breaker:** Automatically disables a Key/Provider on 401, 402, 429, or 5xx errors for a configurable cooldown period.
- **Quota Tracking:** Monitors token usage per key to stay under provider limits.

### 3. Telemetry & Analytics (Redis SSOT)
- **Real-time Stream:** Every request/response is pushed to a Redis Stream (`lmesh:stream`).
- **Global Health Table:** A Redis Hash (`lmesh:health`) storing the current status of all providers/keys.
- **Latency Histograms:** Tracks P50/P90/P95 latency per model.

### 4. Chat Overlay & Control Plane
- **Preset Manager:** Create and switch "Routing Profiles" (e.g., "Aggressive Scalping", "Deep Analysis").
- **Live Dashboard:** Web-based interface showing the flow of tokens and provider health.

## Data Flow
1. **Client** → `POST /v1/chat/completions` (model: "auto:s-tier")
2. **Dispatcher** → Looks up "auto:s-tier" in LMESH Registry.
3. **Registry** → Filters healthy providers (Redis Health check).
4. **Selector** → Picks best Provider/Key based on Latency/Availability Score.
5. **Proxy** → Executes request.
6. **ErrorHandler** → If fails (429/5xx), marks Key as "down" in Redis, triggers immediate fallback to next best candidate.
7. **Telemetry** → Logs metrics to Redis.

- [ ] Simulate 429 error and verify switching to next key/provider

{"content":"# Sprint 0: Foundation

**Goal:** Establish core routing with basic key-loop and circuit breaker.

**Duration:** 1 week (2026-08-30 to 2026-09-05)

## Tasks

### 1. Repository Setup
- [ ] Create new GitHub repository `lmesh` (fork or clean slate)
- [ ] Initialize with MIT license, README, .gitignore
- [ ] Set up basic directory structure: src/, docs/, scripts/
- [ ] Add initial commit with base freellmapi code (copy from submodule)

### 2. Core Infrastructure
- [ ] Set up TypeScript project (if not already) with tsconfig, eslint, prettier
- [ ] Configure Redis client (ioredis) in src/lib/redis.ts
- [ ] Create environment variable loader (src/lib/env.ts)
- [ ] Implement basic Express server setup (copy from freellmapi src/app.ts)

### 3. KeyPoolManager
- [ ] Design KeyPoolManager class:
    - Constructor: accepts provider name, array of API keys
    - Method: `getNextKey()` -> returns next key using round-robin
    - Method: `markKeyFailed(key: string, ttlMs: number)` -> temporarily bans key
    - Method: `isKeyAvailable(key: string)` -> checks if ban expired
- [ ] Write unit tests for KeyPoolManager
- [ ] Integrate KeyPoolManager into provider configuration loading

### 4. Circuit Breaker Integration
- [ ] Extend KeyPoolManager to handle HTTP status codes:
    - On 401, 402, 429 -> mark key as failed with cooldown (e.g., 60s)
    - On 5xx -> optional: mark provider as degraded?
- [ ] Modify proxy request flow to use KeyPoolManager.getNextKey() for each attempt
- [ ] Implement retry loop that tries next key on failure (up to N attempts)

### 5. Telemetry Foundation
- [ ] Create src/lib/telemetry.ts with basic logging to console (later to Redis)
- [ ] Hook telemetry into proxy middleware to log:
    - Timestamp, provider, model, key_id (hash), latency, success/error
- [ ] Ensure no PII logging (avoid logging full prompts/responses)

### 6. Dockerization
- [ ] Write Dockerfile for lmesh (based on node:18-alpine)
- [ ] Create docker-compose.yml for local testing (includes redis)
- [ ] Test: `docker compose up --build` and verify health endpoint

### 7. Verification
- [ ] Start lmesh with a single provider (e.g., Ollama) and two dummy keys
- [ ] Send a request and verify it succeeds
- [ ] Simulate 429 by returning error from first key, verify second key used
- [ ] Simulate 401 on all keys, verify error returned after exhausting pool
- [ ] Check logs for telemetry output

## Definition of Done
- [ ] Code is in new `lmesh` repository (not submodule)
- [ ] Docker image builds and runs successfully
- [ ] KeyPoolManager correctly rotates keys and respects circuit breaker cooldowns
- [ ] Proxy returns successful response when at least one key is valid
- [ ] Telemetry logs basic request metadata to stdout
- [ ] All tasks completed and code reviewed (self-review or partner)

## Notes
- We intentionally delay Redis persistence for telemetry to Sprint 2 to keep this sprint focused.
- The goal is to have a working proxy that can survive key exhaustion/depletion.","file_path":"docs/lmesh/sprints/sprint-0.md"}

Now we need to start implementing Sprint 0 tasks. Let's first look at the server structure to understand where to add the KeyPoolManager.

We'll need to:
1. Create a KeyPoolManager class in src/lib/
2. Modify the provider loading to use multiple keys
3. Update the proxy route to use the KeyPoolManager
4. Add Redis connection (though we might delay Redis to Sprint 2 as per the plan, but for now we can implement in-memory)

Looking at the Sprint 0 plan, we said we'd delay Redis persistence for telemetry to Sprint 2, but for the KeyPoolManager we need to store the banned keys with TTL. We could use an in-memory Map with setTimeout for now, and later replace with Redis.

Let's examine the existing provider configuration. First, look at config/providers.json or similar.

1: import type { Db } from '../db/types.js';

3: export type CatalogModelKind = 'chat' | 'media';
4: 
5: export interface ModelOverridePatch {
6:   displayName?: string;
7:   intelligenceRank?: number;
8:   speedRank?: number;
9:   sizeLabel?: string;
10:   rpmLimit?: number | null;
11:   rpdLimit?: number | null;

14:   monthlyTokenBudget?: string;

16:   supportsVision?: boolean;
17:   supportsTools?: boolean;
18:   enabled?: boolean;
19: }
20: 
21: type StoredOverrides = Partial<ModelOverridePatch>;
22: 
23: const OVERRIDE_COLUMNS: Record<keyof ModelOverridePatch, string> = {
24:   displayName: 'display_name',
25:   intelligenceRank: 'intelligence_rank',
26:   speedRank: 'speed_rank',
27:   sizeLabel: 'size_label',
28:   rpmLimit: 'rpm_limit',
29:   rpdLimit: 'rpd_limit',
30:   tpmLimit: 'tpm_limit',
31:   tpdLimit: 'tpd_limit',
32:   monthlyTokenBudget: 'monthly_token_budget',
33:   contextWindow: 'context_window',
34:   supportsVision: 'supports_vision',
35:   supportsTools: 'supports_tools',
36:   enabled: 'enabled',
37: };
38: 
39: function parseOverrides(raw: string | undefined): StoredOverrides {
40:   if (!raw) return {};
41:   try {
42:     const parsed = JSON.parse(raw) as unknown;
43:     return parsed && typeof parsed === 'object' ? parsed as StoredOverrides : {};
44:   } catch {
45:     return {};
46:   }
47: }
48: 
49: function toDbValue(key: keyof ModelOverridePatch, value: unknown): unknown {
50:   if (key === 'supportsVision' || key === 'supportsTools' || key === 'enabled') return value ? 1 : 0;
51:   return value;
52: }
53: 
54: function cleanPatch(patch: ModelOverridePatch): StoredOverrides {
55:   const cleaned: StoredOverrides = {};
56:   for (const key of Object.keys(OVERRIDE_COLUMNS) as Array<keyof ModelOverridePatch>) {
57:     if (Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(patch, key)) {
58:       cleaned[key] = patch[key] as never;
59:     }
60:   }
61:   return cleaned;
62: }
63: 
64: /**
65:  * The fields a stored overrides blob actually overrides, for callers that
66:  * already selected `model_overrides.overrides_json` alongside the model row.
67:  * The dashboard uses this to mark individual inputs as locally overridden
68:  * instead of flagging the whole model (#551).
69:  */
70: export function overriddenFieldNames(overridesJson: string | null | undefined): Array<keyof ModelOverridePatch> {
71:   const stored = parseOverrides(overridesJson ?? undefined);
72:   return (Object.keys(stored) as Array<keyof ModelOverridePatch>).filter(key => key in OVERRIDE_COLUMNS);
73: }
74: 
75: export function isCatalogManagedModel(row: { platform: string; key_id?: number | null; source?: string }): boolean {
76:   // `source` is the authoritative provenance (models.source, 'catalog'|'user');
77:   // callers that select it get an exact answer. The platform/key_id fallback
78:   // covers callers that don't have the column in hand.
79:   if (row.source === 'user') return false;
80:   return row.platform !== 'custom' && row.key_id == null;
81: }
82: 
83: // Why a catalog model carries a tombstone:
84: //   'user'        — deleted in the dashboard. Stays deleted across syncs, and
85: //                   the row is removed from `models` on the next catalog apply.
86: //   'upstream_eol' — the provider reported it permanently gone (410 / end of
87: //                   life, issue #634). The row SURVIVES and is only disabled,
88: //                   so the dashboard can show "retired upstream" instead of
89: //                   silently losing the model, and so a later catalog that
90: //                   still lists it can lift the retirement.
91: export type CatalogTombstoneSource = 'user' | 'upstream_eol';
92: 
93: export interface CatalogModelTombstone {
94:   source: CatalogTombstoneSource;
95:   reason: string | null;
96:   createdAt: string;
97: }
98: 
99: export function getCatalogModelTombstone(
100:   db: Db,
101:   kind: CatalogModelKind,
102:   platform: string,
103:   modelId: string,
104: ): CatalogModelTombstone | undefined {
105:   const row = db
106:     .prepare('SELECT source, reason, created_at FROM catalog_model_tombstones WHERE kind = ? AND platform = ? AND model_id = ?')
107:     .get(kind, platform, modelId) as { source: string; reason: string | null; created_at: string } | undefined;
108:   if (!row) return undefined;
109:   return {
110:     source: row.source === 'upstream_eol' ? 'upstream_eol' : 'user',
111:     reason: row.reason ?? null,
112:     createdAt: row.created_at,
113:   };
114: }
115: 
116: /**
117:  * True only for models the USER deleted — the "keep it deleted" contract every
118:  * caller here means. An upstream-retirement tombstone deliberately does NOT
119:  * count: those models stay in the catalog's write path so a refreshed catalog
120:  * can reinstate them (see reinstateUpstreamRetiredCatalogModel).
121:  */
122: export function isCatalogModelTombstoned(
123:   db: Db,
124:   kind: CatalogModelKind,
125:   platform: string,
126:   modelId: string,
127: ): boolean {
128:   return getCatalogModelTombstone(db, kind, platform, modelId)?.source === 'user';
129: }
130: 
131: export function recordCatalogModelTombstone(
132:   db: Db,
133:   kind: CatalogModelKind,
134:   platform: string,
135:   modelId: string,
136:   options: { source?: CatalogTombstoneSource; reason?: string | null } = {},
137: ): void {
138:   const source: CatalogTombstoneSource = options.source ?? 'user';
139:   db.prepare(`
140:     INSERT INTO catalog_model_tombstones (kind, platform, model_id, source, reason)
141:     VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)
142:     ON CONFLICT(kind, platform, model_id)
143:     DO UPDATE SET created_at = datetime('now'), source = excluded.source, reason = excluded.reason
144:   `).run(kind, platform, modelId, source, options.reason ?? null);

1: /**
2:  * Express router handles model fallback configuration and token budget reporting.
3:  * It integrates named profiles dynamically into the fallback routing logic and aggregates
4:  * monthly token consumption and rate limits (RPM/RPD/TPM/TPD) across configured models.
5:  */
6: import { Router } from 'express';
7: import type { Request, Response } from 'express';
8: import { z } from 'zod';
9: import { getDb } from '../db/index.js';
10: import { getAllPenalties, getRoutingScores, getRoutingStrategy, setRoutingStrategy, setCustomWeights, getExploreEnabled, setExploreEnabled, getPeakHoursConfig, setPeakHoursConfig, getActiveRoutingWeights, getKeySelectionStrategy, setKeySelectionStrategy } from '../services/router.js';
11: import { BANDIT_PRESETS, isValidTimezone, type RoutingStrategy } from '../services/scoring.js';
12: import { parseBudget } from '../lib/budget.js';
13: import { getModelGroups } from '../services/model-groups.js';
14: import { getPenaltyInspector } from '../services/penalty-inspector.js';
15: import { getActiveProfileId } from '../services/profile-models.js';

20: export const fallbackRouter = Router();
21: 
22: // ── Bandit routing strategy ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
23: // GET  /routing → active strategy, preset weights, and the per-model score
24: //                 breakdown (reliability / speed / intelligence + guardrails).
25: fallbackRouter.get('/routing', (_req: Request, res: Response) => {
26:   const { peakHours, ...rest } = getRoutingScores();
27:   res.json({
28:     ...rest,
29:     peakHoursAdjust: peakHours.enabled,
30:     peakStartHour: peakHours.startHour,
31:     peakEndHour: peakHours.endHour,
32:     peakTimezone: peakHours.timezone,
33:   });
34: });
35: 
36: fallbackRouter.get('/penalty-inspector', (_req: Request, res: Response) => {
37:   res.json(getPenaltyInspector());
38: });
39: 
40: const routingSchema = z.object({
41:   strategy: z.enum(['priority', 'balanced', 'smartest', 'fastest', 'reliable', 'custom']),
42:   // Only meaningful with strategy 'custom': the user's weight vector. Any
43:   // non-negative vector is accepted; setCustomWeights renormalizes to sum 1.
44:   weights: z.object({
45:     reliability: z.number().nonnegative(),
46:     speed: z.number().nonnegative(),
47:     intelligence: z.number().nonnegative(),
48:   }).optional(),
49:   // Exploration toggle: give unmeasured models a guaranteed chance to be tried.
50:   exploreEnabled: z.boolean().optional(),
51:   // Peak-hours adjustment (#760), off by default. Hours are whole numbers in
52:   // 0-23 and are read in `peakTimezone`, never the server's local clock, so the
53:   // window means the same thing on a UTC container as on the operator's laptop.
54:   peakHoursAdjust: z.boolean().optional(),
55:   peakStartHour: z.number().int().min(0).max(23, { message: 'peakStartHour must be an integer between 0 and 23' }).optional(),
56:   peakEndHour: z.number().int().min(0).max(23, { message: 'peakEndHour must be an integer between 0 and 23' }).optional(),
57:   peakTimezone: z.string().refine(isValidTimezone, { message: 'peakTimezone must be a valid IANA timezone name' }).optional(),
58:   // How to pick between several keys of one platform (#919). Independent of
59:   // `strategy`, which ranks MODELS — the two are set from the same form, so
60:   // they round-trip through the same request.
61:   keySelectionStrategy: z.enum(['auto', 'least-remaining']).optional(),
62: });
63: 
64: // PUT /routing → switch strategy. Presets are just weight vectors over the three
65: // axes; 'priority' falls back to the legacy manual chain order; 'custom' uses
66: // the user's saved weights (optionally updated in the same request).
67: fallbackRouter.put('/routing', (req: Request, res: Response) => {
68:   const parsed = routingSchema.safeParse(req.body);
69:   if (!parsed.success) {
70:     res.status(400).json({ error: { message: parsed.error.errors.map(e => e.message).join(', ') } });
71:     return;
72:   }
73:   // Persist the weights before flipping the strategy so the new mode reads the
74:   // intended vector immediately. setCustomWeights throws on an all-zero vector.
75:   if (parsed.data.weights) {
76:     try {
77:       setCustomWeights(parsed.data.weights);
78:     } catch (err: any) {
79:       res.status(400).json({ error: { message: err?.message ?? 'Invalid custom weights' } });
80:       return;
81:     }
82:   }
83:   setRoutingStrategy(parsed.data.strategy as RoutingStrategy);
84:   if (parsed.data.exploreEnabled !== undefined) {
85:     setExploreEnabled(parsed.data.exploreEnabled);
86:   }
87:   if (parsed.data.keySelectionStrategy !== undefined) {
88:     setKeySelectionStrategy(parsed.data.keySelectionStrategy);
89:   }
90:   try {
91:     setPeakHoursConfig({
92:       enabled: parsed.data.peakHoursAdjust,
93:       startHour: parsed.data.peakStartHour,
94:       endHour: parsed.data.peakEndHour,
95:       timezone: parsed.data.peakTimezone,
96:     });
97:   } catch (err: any) {
98:     res.status(400).json({ error: { message: err?.message ?? 'Invalid peak-hours settings' } });
99:     return;
100:   }
101:   // `presets` is the raw preset table (unchanged); `weights` is what the router
102:   // will actually use right now, which differs from the preset while the
103:   // peak-hours adjustment is firing. Returning both keeps the echo honest
104:   // without breaking clients that read `presets` (#760).
105:   const active = getActiveRoutingWeights();
106:   const peak = getPeakHoursConfig();
107:   res.json({
108:     strategy: getRoutingStrategy(),
109:     exploreEnabled: getExploreEnabled(),
110:     keySelectionStrategy: getKeySelectionStrategy(),
111:     presets: BANDIT_PRESETS,
112:     weights: active.weights,
113:     peakAdjusted: active.adjusted,
114:     peakHoursAdjust: peak.enabled,
115:     peakStartHour: peak.startHour,
116:     peakEndHour: peak.endHour,
117:     peakTimezone: peak.timezone,
118:   });
119: });

121: // The catalog columns every fallback row carries, whichever table supplies the
122: // priority/enabled pair. Kept in one place so the profile and the no-profile
123: // query can never drift apart.
124: const MODEL_COLUMNS = `
125:            m.platform, m.model_id, m.display_name, m.intelligence_rank,
126:            m.speed_rank, m.size_label, m.rpm_limit, m.rpd_limit,
127:            m.tpm_limit, m.tpd_limit, m.context_window,
128:            m.monthly_token_budget, m.supports_vision, m.supports_tools,
129:            m.key_id, m.endpoint_scope, ak.label AS key_label,
130:            mo.overrides_json IS NOT NULL AS has_overrides,
131:            mo.overrides_json,
132:            ts.source AS tombstone_source, ts.reason AS tombstone_reason`;
133: 
134: const MODEL_JOINS = `
135:     LEFT JOIN api_keys ak ON ak.id = m.key_id
136:     LEFT JOIN model_overrides mo ON mo.platform = m.platform AND mo.model_id = m.model_id
137:     LEFT JOIN catalog_model_tombstones ts
138:       ON ts.kind = 'chat' AND ts.platform = m.platform AND ts.model_id = m.model_id`;
139: 
140: // The whole catalog seen THROUGH one chain (#1021). A chain is a set of opt-ins,
141: // not a copy of the catalog: a model the chain names keeps the priority and the
142: // on/off flag stored against it, and a model it does not name is still listed —
143: // switched OFF, ranked after everything the chain does name. That is what makes
144: // a hand-built ("start empty") chain usable at all: it renders as "the catalog,
145: // nothing turned on yet" instead of an empty page, and turning a row on is the
146: // PUT below, which writes the row into the chain. Nothing is persisted by GET.
147: const PROFILE_CHAIN_SQL = `
148:     SELECT m.id AS model_db_id, pm.priority AS chain_priority, pm.enabled AS chain_enabled,
149:            fc.priority AS catalog_priority,
150: ${MODEL_COLUMNS}
151:     FROM models m
152:     LEFT JOIN profile_models pm ON pm.profile_id = ? AND pm.model_db_id = m.id
153:     LEFT JOIN fallback_config fc ON fc.model_db_id = m.id
154: ${MODEL_JOINS}
155:     WHERE m.enabled = 1
156: `;
157: 
158: const GLOBAL_CHAIN_SQL = `
159:     SELECT fc.model_db_id, fc.priority, fc.enabled,
160: ${MODEL_COLUMNS}
161:     FROM fallback_config fc
162:     JOIN models m ON m.id = fc.model_db_id
163: ${MODEL_JOINS}
164:     WHERE m.enabled = 1
165:     ORDER BY fc.priority ASC
166: `;

168: /**
169:  * Order a chain-scoped catalog read and give every row a priority.
170:  *
171:  * Rows the chain names come first, in their stored order and keeping their
172:  * stored numbers. Rows it does not name follow in catalog order, numbered after
173:  * the last stored one, so the list stays monotonic and stable between reads
174:  * without writing anything back.
175:  */
176: function orderProfileRows(rows: any[]): any[] {
177:   const inChain = rows.filter(r => r.chain_priority != null);
178:   const rest = rows.filter(r => r.chain_priority == null);
179:   inChain.sort((a, b) => a.chain_priority - b.chain_priority || a.model_db_id - b.model_db_id);
180:   rest.sort((a, b) =>
181:     (a.catalog_priority ?? Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER) - (b.catalog_priority ?? Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER)
182:     || a.model_db_id - b.model_db_id);
183: 
184:   const maxStored = inChain.length ? inChain[inChain.length - 1].chain_priority : 0;
185:   return [
186:     ...inChain.map(r => ({ ...r, priority: r.chain_priority, enabled: r.chain_enabled })),
187:     ...rest.map((r, i) => ({ ...r, priority: maxStored + 1 + i, enabled: 0 })),
188:   ];
189: }

192: fallbackRouter.get('/', (_req: Request, res: Response) => {
193:   const db = getDb();

197:   // through to the global table there is what made two different empty chains
198:   // show (and save) the same configuration (#1021).

203:   // Count usable keys per platform — enabled AND healthy/unknown status. Unified
204:   // with /token-usage and the routing scorer (#456) so budget pooling is computed
205:   // from the same key set everywhere (a disabled or invalid key adds no capacity).
206:   const keyCounts = db.prepare(`

359: function getBudgetScore(m: { monthly_token_budget: string; tpd_limit: number | null }): number {

377:   else if (upper.includes('K')) mult = 1_000;

379:   return maxNum * mult;

520: // Per-model time-window rate-limit usage (RPM/RPD/TPM: used vs limit), for the
521: // dashboard's remaining-quota display (#876). The monthly-budget metric says
522: // nothing about windowed limits, so this surfaces what the router actually
523: // enforces.
524: //
525: // Which key's numbers to report matters. The badge answers "how close is this
526: // model to being unroutable", so it has to follow the key the router would pick
527: // NEXT, not the worst key on the account: a platform with one exhausted key and
528: // one idle key routes fine, and reporting the exhausted one paints a red badge
529: // over a model that is wide open. So we mirror the router's key eligibility
530: // (`selectKeyForModel`) — enabled + healthy/unknown, model scope allows this
531: // model (#657), and for a custom model the key must belong to the model's own
532: // endpoint (#212, #619) — and then report the ELIGIBLE key with the most
533: // headroom (lowest used/limit ratio across its windows), which is the key the
534: // router lands on once the busier ones fail their gates.
535: //
536: // Cost: the naive shape is three SQL counts per model × key, which is thousands
537: // of statements on a real catalog. All of it comes from one table, so the whole
538: // page is a single grouped scan of `rate_limit_usage` over the last day.
539: const RATE_LIMIT_MINUTE_MS = 60 * 1000;
540: const RATE_LIMIT_DAY_MS = 24 * 60 * RATE_LIMIT_MINUTE_MS;

542: interface KeyUsage { rpm: number; rpd: number; tpm: number }
543: const NO_USAGE: KeyUsage = { rpm: 0, rpd: 0, tpm: 0 };
544: 
545: /** used/limit for one window, or null when the model has no such limit. */
546: function windowRatio(used: number, limit: number | null): number | null {
547:   if (limit == null || limit <= 0) return null;
548:   return used / limit;
549: }
550: 
551: /** The busiest window of one key: what would reject this key's next request. */
552: function keyPressure(usage: KeyUsage, limits: { rpm: number | null; rpd: number | null; tpm: number | null }): number {
553:   let worst = 0;
554:   for (const r of [
555:     windowRatio(usage.rpm, limits.rpm),
556:     windowRatio(usage.rpd, limits.rpd),
557:     windowRatio(usage.tpm, limits.tpm),
558:   ]) {
559:     if (r !== null && r > worst) worst = r;
560:   }
561:   return worst;
562: }

lines.text: * Express router handles model fallback configuration and token budget reporting.
* It integrates named profiles dynamically into the fallback routing logic and aggregates
* monthly token consumption and rate limits (RPM/RPD/TPM/TPD) across configured models.

import { getAllPenalties, getRoutingScores, getRoutingStrategy, setRoutingStrategy, setCustomWeights, getExploreEnabled, setExploreEnabled, getPeakHoursConfig, setPeakHoursConfig, getActiveRoutingWeights, getKeySelectionStrategy, setKeySelectionStrategy } from '../services/router.js';
import { BANDIT_PRESETS, isValidTimezone, type RoutingStrategy } from '../services/scoring.js';
// GET  /routing → active strategy, preset weights, and the per-model score
// Only meaningful with strategy 'custom': the user's weight vector. Any
// non-negative vector is accepted; setCustomWeights renormalizes to sum 1.
// Exploration toggle: give unmeasured models a guaranteed chance to be tried.
// Peak-hours adjustment (#760), off by default. Hours are whole numbers in
// 0-23 and are read in `peakTimezone`, never the server's local clock, so the
// window means the same thing on a UTC container as on the operator's laptop.
peakStartHour: z.number().int().min(0).max(23, { message: 'peakStartHour must be an integer between 0 and 23' }).optional(),
peakEndHour: z.number().int().min(0).max(23, { message: 'peakEndHour must be an integer between 0 and 23' }).optional(),
peakTimezone: z.string().refine(isValidTimezone, { message: 'peakTimezone must be a valid IANA timezone name' }).optional(),
// How to pick between several keys of one platform (#919). Independent of

233: function getSessionKey(messages: ChatMessage[], sessionIdHeader?: string, strategyKey?: string): string {
234:   if (sessionIdHeader) {
235:     return strategyKey ? `hdr:${sessionIdHeader}::${strategyKey}` : `hdr:${sessionIdHeader}`;
236:   }
237: 
238:   const firstUser = messages.find(m => m.role === 'user');
239:   if (!firstUser) return '';
240:   const text = contentToString(firstUser.content ?? '');
241:   if (!text) return '';
242:   const payload = strategyKey ? `${text}::${strategyKey}` : text;
243:   return crypto.createHash('sha1').update(payload).digest('hex');
244: }
245: 
246: export function getStickyModel(messages: ChatMessage[], sessionIdHeader?: string, strategyKey?: string): number | undefined {
247:   const hasAssistant = messages.some(m => m.role === 'assistant');
248:   if (!hasAssistant) return undefined;
249: 
250:   const key = getSessionKey(messages, sessionIdHeader, strategyKey);
251:   if (!key) return undefined;
252: 
253:   const entry = stickySessionMap.get(key);
254:   if (!entry) return undefined;
255: 
256:   if (Date.now() - entry.lastUsed > STICKY_TTL_MS) {
257:     stickySessionMap.delete(key);
258:     return undefined;
259:   }
260:   return entry.modelDbId;
261: }
262: 
263: export function setStickyModel(messages: ChatMessage[], modelDbId: number, sessionIdHeader?: string, strategyKey?: string) {
264:   const key = getSessionKey(messages, sessionIdHeader, strategyKey);
265:   if (!key) return;
266:   stickySessionMap.set(key, { modelDbId, lastUsed: Date.now() });
267: 
268:   // Cleanup old entries
269:   if (stickySessionMap.size > 500) {
270:     const now = Date.now();
271:     for (const [k, v] of stickySessionMap) {
272:       if (now - v.lastUsed > STICKY_TTL_MS) stickySessionMap.delete(k);
273:     }
274: 
275:     // Hard cap: if still over 1000 after pruning expired entries, evict oldest by lastUsed
276:     if (stickySessionMap.size > 1000) {
277:       const entries = [...stickySessionMap.entries()].sort(
278:         (a, b) => a[1].lastUsed - b[1].lastUsed
279:       );
280:       const toEvict = stickySessionMap.size - 1000;
281:       for (let i = 0; i < toEvict; i++) {
282:         stickySessionMap.delete(entries[i][0]);
283:       }
284:     }
285:   }
286: }

294:   // with whether it is currently usable, so a client can see everything and know
295:   // what's connected vs. disabled/keyless (#242). `?available=true` (aliases
296:   // `?connected=true`, `?ready=true`) narrows the list to only models that can
297:   // serve a request right now — the previous default behavior. The `ready`
298:   // alias is the machine-readable filter a meta-gateway uses (#433) to ask
299:   // "which models can this instance actually serve now". `available` is computed as
300:   // "enabled AND an enabled key can serve it"; dedup prefers an available
301:   // instance of a model id over a disabled/keyless one.
302:   // Shared catalog listing (one source of truth for the OpenAI and Anthropic
303:   // /v1/models endpoints — see services/model-listing.ts). `autoContextWindow`
304:   // is the honest ceiling for the virtual "auto" model: the largest context
305:   // window among models that can serve a request right now. Advertising null
306:   // makes OpenAI-compatible clients (opencode, Continue) fall back to their own
307:   // conservative default and truncate long inputs before they reach us (#282).
308:   const { models: allListed, autoContextWindow } = buildModelListing();
309: 
310:   const q = String(req.query.available ?? req.query.connected ?? req.query.ready ?? '').toLowerCase();
311:   const onlyAvailable = q === '1' || q === 'true' || q === 'yes';
312:   const listed = onlyAvailable ? allListed.filter(m => m.available === 1) : allListed;
313: 
314:   // Named fallback chains (#960/#895): every user-defined profile is exposed
315:   // as an `auto:<name>` model so a client can pick a specific fallback chain
316:   // per request (auto:my-group) instead of only the active one. Available iff
317:   // at least one model in that profile's chain can serve a request right now.
318:   const profileRows = getDb().prepare(`
319:     SELECT p.id, p.name,
320:            EXISTS (
321:              SELECT 1
322:              FROM profile_models pm
323:              JOIN models m ON m.id = pm.model_db_id AND m.enabled = 1
324:              WHERE pm.profile_id = p.id AND pm.enabled = 1
325:                AND EXISTS (
326:                  SELECT 1 FROM api_keys k
327:                  WHERE k.platform = m.platform AND k.enabled = 1
328:                    AND (m.key_id IS NULL OR k.id = m.key_id)
329:                )
330:            ) AS usable,
331:            (SELECT MAX(m2.context_window)
332:             FROM profile_models pm2
333:             JOIN models m2 ON m2.id = pm2.model_db_id AND m2.enabled = 1
334:             WHERE pm2.profile_id = p.id AND pm2.enabled = 1) AS max_ctx
335:     FROM profiles p
336:     WHERE p.type = 'custom'

340:   // Claude-family discovery entries (#880). The Anthropic-shaped GET /v1/models

348:   // something can actually serve them, and never when the id would collide

352:     ? claudeFamilyDiscoveryEntries()
